blocks.text: To start the study of arithmetic it is worth first to review the three period lesson as presented in the Discovery of the Child. For the first period (association), the guide should present only the necessary words in a clear voice without adding any other extra words. For the second period (recognition of the name with the object): the guide will check if the name has remained associated with the object in the child’s memory. Between the first and the second period a few moments of silence are required. This second period is the most important of all, as it contains the real lesson, the real mnemonic and associative aid. If the second period is not successful the guide should suspend the lesson without correcting the child and get back to it in
ther moment. The third period (remembering the name corresponding to the object)
is a rapid verification of the lesson first given. The guide asks the child to name the
bject, but if the guide can notice some insecurity, he can repeat the second period
to help the child feel more comfortable.

The numerical limit for this group is ten. This group is divided in two sub groups with the first subgroup in which the units are joined (Number rods, Sandpaper digits) and the second subgroup in which the units are separated (Spindle boxes, Cards and Counters and Memory Game of Numbers). In Children’s house, these presentations are individual but for the special 6 years old, the presentations are a little bit different. It is important to give the special 6 years old a clear idea of number in relation with quantity. The aim will be to bring order and clarity with the numbers that he might already know when he comes to Elementary school. Psychologists say that the children at this age have an interest to put the objects in order.
Ten wooden rods painted in blue and red, the same as the long rods apart from the colour. The shortest rod is 10 cm long and the longest rod is 1m. All the rods start with the blue colour.
The guide invites the children to join and take the rods to a mat.
The guide separates the first 3.
First period
The guide points to the rod of 1 and says “This is one”.
The guide points to the rod of 2 and says “This is two”, counts and shows to the child how rod one is inside the rode number 2.
Second period
The guide asks the child to point to the number 2.
Third period
The guide asks the child what number is this one by pointing to a rod.
The guide will encourage the child to trace while counting.
The guide will continue in the same day or another moment until all the rods are presented.
Game one (Distance game)
The guide puts the rods in a random order on a mat at distance and asks the child to bring a rod by saying “Please bring me the rod of 5”.
When the child brings the rod, the guide counts again with the rod.
We can continue as long as the child is interested.
Game two (Distance game “Before/after the rod of”)
The guides puts the rods in a random order on a mat at distance and asks the child to bring a rod by saying, “Please bring me the rod that comes immediately before the rod of 8”.
When the child brings the rod the guide counts again with the rod.
We can continue as long as the child is interested. It is important for the child to count.
Game three (Sort the rods in order)
The guides puts the rods in a random order on a mat. The order starts from one to ten from the bottom to the top.
The guide shows the child how to start and lets him continue, as it is easy because the material has a clear control of error.
Learn the name related to the quantities
Learn the numerical sequence from 1 to 10
Preparation for the metric system (first rod is 1 decimeter and the longest 1 meter). When we introduce the measurements, the child will return to this material to measure objects.
When looking at the rods we can think of the rods as ordinal numbers (first, second, etc.). We can even play a game with the ordinal numbers so the children can familiarize with the ordinal numbers.
6 years old
With the digits of the decimal system, it is possible to write any number.

10 sandpapers numbers/digits that are made of 10 smooth cards with the digit made from sandpaper from 0 to 9. The digits are placed a little bit off-center so he can hold the card with the left hand and trace with the right. Ideally, the cards should have space on both sides.
The guide invites the child to pick up the work and names it “Sandpaper digits”. The child takes the work to a table.
First period
When the guide introduces the first time the sandpaper digits, the guide will remove momentarily the card with zero.
The guide takes the card with 1, says “This is one”, traces the card and invites the child to do the same. The guide continues up to 3 cards.
Second period
The guide asks the child to show him 1.”Can you show me 1?”
Third period
The guide asks the child “What number is this?”
Give the child the numerical symbol for the quantities that they already know.
Preparation for the writing of the numbers.
The children will notice that the number 10 is missing and this will give us the passage to the next work “Number rods and cards”
There is a set of wallpaper sandpaper digits that after the introduction of 0 can be hanged on the wall.
6 years old
Ten wooden rods painted in blue and red, the same as the long rods apart from the colour. The shortest is 10 cm long and the longest rod is 1m. All the rods start with the blue colour.
A box with cards with the numbers from 1 to 10. The card of 10 it has the double width compared to the card of 1.
The guide invites the children to join and take the rods to a mat and the cards. The guide ask the child to put the rods in order as presented before.
As the children already know the rods and the numbers from 1 to 9. So number 10 is the only unknown
The guide says “This is the number 10. Look how I place it on the rod of 10”
The guide invites the child to count and place the other cards.
Game one (“Match”)
The guide places the cards on a mat and the rods on another mat both in random order.
The guide asks the child to bring the number 7.
The guide gives a rod to the child and asks the child to check if it’s right. Now the child can choose the card and find the corresponding rod, the guide always checks by counting.
Game two (“Making the rod of 10”)
The guide asks the child to put the rods in order.
The guide says “Let’s make today all the rods as long as the one of 10”. Shows the 9+1 and invites the child to go ahead.
The rod of 5 is left alone, so the guide shows how you can flip to the other side to make 10.
The guide removes the rod of 4 and places it to its place. The child can continue till all the rods are back in order.
Association of number and symbol
Preparation for addition, subtraction and multiplication.
6 years old

In this work, it is the first time that the children work with the number 0. Maria Montessori said that the children should understand what the number 0 means. The guide can introduce this concept after doing the spindle box presentation with a game like the
ne Maria Montessori described in the “The Discovery of the Child” (The game of zero).
Two boxes with five compartment each, with the numbers from 0 to 9 printed
n the back of the compartment
A box/basket with 45 spindles
8 binders/ribbons/elastics
Sandpaper digit 0.
The guide introduces the material name and asks the child to bring the spindle boxes on a mat.

The guide asks the child to read the numbers that he knows from the back of the compartments. The guide shows the number 0 and can make a short lesson about the number 0. The guide will also use the sandpaper digit 0 to show to the child how to trace it. (This presentation should be done after the child finished using the spindle boxes).
The guide invites the child to place the spindles in the respective compartments.
When the child has finished placing the spindles, the guide shows to the child how to use the elastic to keep the spindles for each number together while counting again for each number.
Introduction of the concept of 0.
Tying the spindles together gives the child the idea that a certain number of units forms the number.
With the number rods, we introduce the child to the decimal system but with the spindle boxes, we see that after 9 we have superior hierarchies.
The symbols presented in the spindle boxes are the digits that we need for writing any number in the decimal system.
6 years old
55 counters
A box with the cards with numbers from 1 to 10
The guide invites the child to join, introduces the name of the work and asks the child to place it on a mat.
As by this time the child knows the numbers and the symbols this work serves more as a verification.
The guide asks the child to place the cards from 1 to 10 on the mat in order
The guide invites the child to place the counters according to the number shown on the card
When the child is done the guide says that will help the child to check and shows to the child how to order the counters, placing them in pairs of 2
Game one (Pass / Can’t pass)
First period
The guide shows the child with the index finger that there are some numbers where the finger can pass between the counters.
The guide says: “The numbers where you can pass are called even and the ones where you can’t pass are called odd.”
Second period
Invites the child to say if he can pass or no
The guide invites the child to read the odd numbers
Another game is to flip the cards and ask the child to say the even numbers so the child will see how one number is always skipped.
Now it’s the time for the odd numbers. “Please turn the cards of all the
dd number”
Third period
The guide takes the counters away asks the child to read the even numbers and later the odd numbers
Game two (Remember the numbers even/odd)
The guide asks the child to remember the odd numbers
The guide asks the child to remember the even numbers
Verify that the child knows the sequence of the numerical symbols from 1 to 10
Learn to distinguish the even and odd numbers.
Preparations to know that all the numbers that end with an odd digit are odd and the ones ending with the even digits are even numbers (0 included here).
Preparation for the divisibility by 2 – all even numbers are divisible by 2.

As we saw with the three period lesson, if we have to apply it to this cycle of work, the number rods are the first period – the association, the second period is the spindle boxes – the recognition and for the third period are the cards and counters for the remembering
6 years old
One box with 55 identical objects
11 folded cards with the numbers from 0 to 10
The guide asks the child to choose a folded card, have a look but hide it from the others
The guide asks the children to take the corresponding number of objects they need but by leaving the card behind – and have to hide it from the others
When all the children are done, the guide asks the children to place the objects in front of their card. The guide will ask and makes an emphasis of the card with zero.
The child trains his memory to pick up the right amount
Memory and recognition of matching symbols and quantities
If there is an error at the end the guide can ask the children to play again instead of trying to find out who made a mistake
6 years old

children.title: First snake game (Snake game for the search of 10)

blocks.text: 1 box with colour beads bars from 1 to 9 (10 bars for each number)
1: red
2: green
3: pink
4: yellow
5: blue
6: brown
7: white
8: light blue
9: dark blue
1 box with golden beads bars of 10 (10 bars)
1 box with black and white beads bars (exchange bars/remainder bars) and 1 counter/bridge
1: 1 black bead
2: 2 black beads
3: 3 black beads
4: 4 black beads
5: 5 black beads
6: 5 black beads and 1 white bead
7: 5 black beads and 2 white beads
8: 5 black beads and 3 white beads
9: 5 black beads and 4 white beads
The guide invites the child to join, introduces the name of the work and asks the child to place it on a table
The guide introduces each coloured bead and says: “This is one”/” “This is two”/ “This is three”/ “This is four”
The guide makes a three period lesson
When the child knows the number, the guide will introduce the colours
The guide can play a short game. “Do you remember what colour is 3?”
The guide says: “Today I’m going to show a special bead bar”. “Would you like to count the beads of this bar?”
The child counts
The guide says that this is ” the golden bead bar”
The guide says “I can show you a new box of beads. These are the strange bead bars. Let me show you why are strange …” “Look 1 is black, the 2 is black, 4 is black, 5 is black as well”
The guide explains the beads bar of 6 which is white and black
The guide shows the beads bars of 7, 8, 9 in an attractive manner for the child
The guide will invite the child to play a game with the bead bars from 6 to 9 – the guide will play the game a few times
Presentation of the snake game
The guide will start building a snake with the colour bead bars
The first snake should have a few tens at the beginning and should be a number made of tens at the end (E.g. 3,7,2,8,7,5,3,6,9,5,2,3)
After the snake was built the guide closes the colour bead bar box
The guide opens the golden beads box and leaves the lid on the side
The guide takes out the black and white bead bars and makes a pyramid
The guide makes a short fun introduction “The snake changes the skin”
The guide explain that to change the colour bead bars it has to be done in a certain way with the help of the bridge
The guide shows how to count to 10 and place the bridge down when reaches 10
The guide replaces the 10 beads with a golden bead bar and puts the colour bead bars in the empty lid of the golden bead bars
The guide starts counting again, reaches 10 but cannot change the last bar so it replaces the uncounted beads with the corresponding black and white bead bar and places the golden bead bars.
The guide continues till all the colour beads have been counted
After finishing the guide counts the golden bead bars
The guide asks the child to check together if it’s the same snake
The guide takes the colour bead bars and orders them from largest to smallest
The guide takes the golden bead bars, puts one on the side horizontally/vertically, and places the necessary colour beads to equal it, under it/next to it.
Repeats till all the colour beads are next/under to the corresponding golden bead bars.
Observations for the snake game

If the snake ends with a colour beads bar that cannot be changed for a golden beads bar, the colour beads bar has to be changed with a black and white beads bar. At the moment of checking at the end we pair the black and white bead bar with the colour beads bar corresponding.
If the guide needs a colour bead bar to make a ten but it is not available the guide changes the colour bead bar with something convenient from the colour beads bars box
Counting to 10
Preparation for addition and subtraction
6 years old

Decimal system is the base on which we order the numerical quantities. Introduced in the medieval times by the Arabs the decimal system has its strength in its simplicity. With just 10 digits (0-9) we can form any possible integral number. Isn’t that fascinating that these 10 digits can take us to explore an infinite number of combinations?

As it is so simple, it makes it great to introduce it even to the young children. With a correct and visual explanation of the decimal system, the child can feel empowered to go on and explore all by himself. Once the child had understood the functioning of the decimal system, counting and calculating are just procedures
ffered by the decimal system.

The root or the foundation of the decimal system has been explained to the child with the pre-elementary materials (zero to nine), now that he has a good understanding of the foundation he can go further with the exploration. The problem arises with the number 10, a moment in which a new order is needed: the
rder of the tens, and once 90 is reached another new order is required: the order of

the hundreds. If we have a quick look at the table presented below, we can see that every time an order gets to the digit 9 a new one starts with the digit 1. The value of these numbers is given not by the digit itself but by its position. The different positions of the numbers are given by placing a 0 at the end, one for the tens, two for the hundreds.

Offering the decimal system, as a material for the child is possible and this material not only offers a simple way to visualize otherwise abstract concepts but it allows the child to work with an exact material/instrument to build the necessary understanding
f the beauty of the decimal system.
hundreds tens units

The material that we are presenting to the children is made of three elements: it is made of objects, numbers and words. The objects are the golden beads. Giving to this material the name of golden beads shows how important is this material for the development of the child. This material is called “the material limited to 9”.
One box with 9 loose golden beads
One box with 9 golden bead bars of 10
One box with 9 golden bead squares of 100
One box with 1 cube of 1000 golden beads
Wooden trays with a small tray inside for the units
One wooden box with:
Set of cards from 1 to 9 in green colour
Set of cards from 10 to 90 in blue colour
Set of cards from 100 to 900 in red colour
Set of cards from 1000 to 9000 in green colour
Presentation of the quantities
The guide places in the tray one unit of 1, one of 10, one
f 100 and one cube of 1000
The guide asks the child what’s the golden bead alone, the guide says “It’s one”
The guide asks the child what’s the golden bead bar of 10, the guide says “It’s ten”
The guide asks the child what’s the golden bead square
f 100, the guide says “It’s hundred”
The guide asks the child what’s the golden bead cube, the guide says “It’s thousand”
The guide makes a short three period lesson with the names introduced
The guide plays a game with the golden bead of one to show that the golden bead of 1 is very small
The guide plays the game again with the golden beads bar of 10 – shows to the child that it’s long
The guide plays the game again with the golden beads bar of 100 – shows to the child that it’s much bigger
The guide plays the game again with the golden beads cube of 1000 – shows to the child that it’s huge
The guide invites the child to show him how the beads bars are formed (10 beads bar has 10 of 1 loose bead / 100 beads bar has 10 bars of 10/ 1000 beads cube has 10 bars of 100 beads)
Presentation of the quantities – additional activity
The guide asks the child to bring him 3 ten golden bead bars
The child brings it and the guide checks the quantity
The guide will repeat until the child feels comfortable with the quantity
Presentation of the symbols
The guide prepares a tray with the cards of 1, 10, 100, and 1000. The card of 1 is placed in the small tray
The guide introduces the cards with the symbols to the child
The guide makes a three period lesson with the child
The guide points out the different colours of the numbers on the cards

The guide play a game to familiarize the child with the colours and with the numbers of the zeros on each card. (E.g. putting the cards face down and asking the child what colour is 1, 10, 100, 1000 and later a game with the cards face down to see how many zeros for 1, 10, 100, 1000.

The guide shows the beautiful cards with the children and shows the cards on top of each other. Can play with the zeros making them appear and disappear. (E.g. “Let’s use this magic powder to make the 0 disappear”.)
Follow-up activities for the presentation of the symbols
Put cards in sequence

The guide puts the cards in sequence starting from 1 to 9, continuing with 10, 20(two tens), 30(three tens)…90(nine tens), 100…900(1 hundred, 2 hundred, 3 hundred…9 hundred” and finally 1000(1 thousand).
The guide can ask the child to recognize the number that he put on the tray. And does a three period lesson with the child and with this numbers.
Presentation of the association of quantity and symbol
For this activity there are necessary two mats
The guide places on the “mat 1” the unit golden beads and counts
The guide places on the “mat 1” the ten golden bead bars and counts
The guide places on the “mat 1” the hundred golden bead squares and counts
The guide places on the “mat 1” the thousand golden bead cube
The guide says: “Look here are all the quantities with which we played before”
The guide places on the “mat 2” the unit symbol cards and counts
The guide places on the “mat 2” the tens symbol cards and counts
The guide places on the “mat 2” the hundreds symbol cards and counts
The guide places on the “mat 2” the thousand symbol card and counts
The guide places a quantity of beads on the tray and asks the child to bring the symbol cards (better if the child places the card on the symbols).
The guide asks the child to count. The activity repeats as many times as necessary. At the beginning only one hierarchy at a time.
As a variation, now the guide can place the symbol cards on a tray and asks the child to bring the corresponding golden beads.
Another variation is to ask the child to bring both.
Different hierarchies
The guide puts the golden beads from different hierarchies on the tray and asks the child to bring the symbol cards
When the child brings the cards he guide places the cards on the left and asks the child to make the magic for the number to appear. From 600->146 All the available hierarchies in a number
The guide will ask for a big number like 1478 and show to the child that in this case the tray is also heavy when the number is big.
One hierarchy missing
Now the guide asks the child to bring 403. The child brings the beads and the guide shows to the child that no one can take the place of 0. The zero appears in red.
Observations for the association of quantity to a symbol
Mario Montessori calls the presentation of the symbol and the quantity a birds- eye view of the decimal system.
We want the children to recognize the quantity and the symbols of the decimal system
Give the possibility to the child of forming large numbers by knowing the numbers from 0 to 9
Preparation for the fundamental concepts of geometry(point, line, surface, solid)
Preparation for the place value of the digits
Preparation for the families of the hierarchies
The importance of the zero in the number, which is the placeholder of the missing hierarchy so that nothing else can take that place
6 years old
Compare the quantities*
This presentation was not offered in the AMI Montessori course. It has been designed to help the guides who work in accordance with the CCSS from the United States of America.
Greater then, less then and equal signs for quantities
Greater then, less then and equal signs for symbol cards
Golden beads material
Wooden trays with a small tray inside for the units
Two wooden boxes with the small symbol cards
Presentation of the comparison
Introduction of the equal sign
The guide invites two children to work. He prepares the symbol cards and invites the bring the quantity indicated by the symbol cards. Both children have the number 5 on the symbol cards.
When the children bring the quantities, he asks each of them to place the quantity on one side of the mat. He asks “Who brought more beads?”
The children say that it is the same quantity.

The guide says that we have a special sign to show this. He takes out the large equal sign, and examines it with the children. On both sides of the sign is the same distance between the lines. He places it in between the quantities.
The guide says “This is the equal sign; it tells us that the quantity on the left side is equal with the one on the right side.”
The guide places the small equal sign between the symbol cards.
The guide invites the children to take back the quantities. He can do one or two more examples with equal quantities, but larger this time.
Introduction of the “greater then” and “less then” signs
The guide invites the children to bring the quantities of 3 and 7.
The children bring the respective quantities and the guide asks which is larger.
The children say 7.
The guide introduces the sign for greater then. He points that one
f the sides of the sign is larger
when the other one. The larger side points to the larger quantity. The guide places the sign between the quantities and another one between the symbol cards.
The guide invites the children to take back the quantities and later does a few more examples with the children.
To introduce the greater then, less then, and equal signs
6 years old
Static operations means that these operations do not involve changing (don’t need to change from one hierarchy to another)
Dynamic operations means that these operations will involve changing from one hierarchy to another.
The operations are going to be done always in order: addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.
When we are using the static operations, the guide must ensure that the quantities given to the children will stay as static operations.
One box with loose golden beads
One box with golden bead bars of 10
One box with golden bead squares of 100 (drawn)
One box with cubes of 1000 golden beads (drawn)
Wooden trays with a small tray inside for the units
On set of cards with symbols of the decimal system and now are going to be called the large decimal cards up to 9000
3 sets of small decimal cards with the thousands up to 3000
Trays with the little tray for the units
A box with all the signs for the operations
Presentation of laying down the materials

The guide invites the children to bring the materials to a mat and lay down the large decimal cards on the mat. (1-9, 10-90, 100-900, 1000-9000). We need a big mat for the bank and small ones for the children.
We ask the child to lay down the small decimal cards on their mats.
The guide prepares the trays for the children with small decimal symbol cards.
The guide invites the children to come to the “bank” and take the quantity of decimal material they require. The guide recommends to the child to put the symbol cards on the quantity.
The guide checks the trays reads the symbols and asks the child to do the magic with the symbol cards
The guide says to the children “look at me what I’m doing”. Puts all the beads quantities together on the red mat and mixes them up. The guide asks the children if they know which their quantity is.
The guide places the material on a tray and asks the child to go and bring the large decimal cards corresponding to the beads on the tray.
The guide can suggest to the child to start counting with the thousands.

When the child comes that guide asks the child to make the magic with the cards and places the cards under the small decimal cards, not before talking about how heavy is now the tray after putting everything together.
The guide says to the child that what they did is an addition. “What did we do with the quantities?” – “ We put them together” - “This is an operation, we made an addition”

The guide shows the children that they have 3 sets of symbols with the small numbers on the mat, and a big one. The guide shows the children the sign for addition and the line – and shows to the children how they should correctly place it.
Observations for the static addition
The red cloth it is used only for the first presentation.
The guide can prepare command cards with static additions with the hierarchal colours.
Optionally the children can used coloured pencils to write down the numbers that they got.
First presentation (nothing is left in the tray)
The guide prepares a large quantity on the tray (E.g. 6895) and another quantities on the children’s trays (E.g. 3521, 1242, 2132)
The guide gives the trays to three children
The guide says: “Look how many things I have on my tray. I’m very rich but also very generous for you to take away from me what you need”.
The guide goes with the tray to a child and asks him what he needs to take and gives to him the quantity
The guide says: “Now my tray is lighter”
The guide goes to the other child and as the child takes his quantity, the guide emphasizes that the tray gets lighter.
When the last the child takes his quantity at the end they guide’s tray remains empty.
The guide says: “Do you know what you did?”, “What we did is another
peration, it is called subtraction. To subtract means to take away.”
Following presentations (something is left in the tray)
The guide prepares the quantity of 4586 on the big tray, on the child’s tray the guide prepares the symbol cards for 3264
The guide invites to come and take away his quantity from the big tray, starting from the ones ideally.
After the child is done the guide places the symbol cards on the mat and says: “Look at what remained on the big tray”, “Can you please go and take the symbol cards for the big tray”
When the child comes back the guide says that this is the subtraction and introduces the name of the subtraction sign “-“
The guide places the correct signs and reads the operation.
The guide prepares three children trays with the same symbol cards on each
f them.
The guide asks the children to take they their quantity without showing to the
thers what they’ve got.
The guide checks the quantities which the children got on their trays
The guide says that it is going to put all their beads together to do a special
peration today.
The guide says that in fact it is nothing special now, it’s just an addition.
The guide asks the children to show their cards and place them on the mat. They discover that are all the same – what’s special is that all are the same.
The guide says:” Can’t I say 1232, one time, two times, three times. We repeated the quantity there times.”
The guide removes two numbers and places a symbol for “3”.
The guide says we can say: “We can say 1232 times 3”.
The guide introduces the multiplication symbol
The guide checks with the children the quantity in the big tray and makes with the large decimal cards the number and puts necessary signs

The guide says: “This operation is called multiplication. When we do multiplication we repeat the number a few times. But remember that we put the numbers together, that’s addition, this is a special addition that we can call multiplication”
The guide prepares on a big tray the quantity and large decimal symbols of 9369.
The guide says “I can’t hardly carry this quantity”
The guide gives three empty trays.
The guide says “I want to share my quantity with you but each of you must receive the same amount”
The guide starts dividing beads of the thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
The guide shows that he’s tray is empty now.
The guide asks the children “Let’s see if you got the same quantity”, asks the children to go and take the small decimal cards corresponding to their beads.
When the children return the guide reads the quantity and emphasizes that the distribution was very good.
The guide says “When I shared that big quantity, it means that I divided that quantity. That big quantity divided in between the three of you is 3123.”
The guide says “This operation we can call it division”.
The guide shows the division sign and says that is important to know in how many parts the quantity has been divided.
The guide places the signs next to the large and small decimal cards.
Observations for the static division
If multiplication was a special addition then division is a special subtraction
The child needs only the ability to count to 9

sections.label: Presentation of the Changing game for the addition

blocks.text: The guide says “Look I’m going to take so many golden beads in this tray”
The guide takes many golden beads and remembers the child the Snake game in which you count only up to 10 and stop
The guide invites the child to start counting and stops the child when he reaches 10
The guide exchanges the child’s loose beads with a bar with a golden bead bar of 10 – asks the child to count the beads on the bar
The game continues until the child counts less than 10
The guide analyzes what the child has on the tray and concludes that it is the same.
The guide starts a game with the golden bead bars of 10 and exchanges the 10 golden bead bars in one golden bead square of 100.
After game with the 10 golden bead bars, the guide can start another with the golden bead squares for the golden bead cubes.
Observations for the changing game for the addition
Show to the child that the highest you can reach is 9, after the number 9 is another hierarchy.
The child has been introduced to this concept as there are beads only up to 9 after this number is a different object
Presentation of addition (dynamic operation)
The guide invites 3 children, 2 are bringing the quantities and the third is checking the quantities (bank).
The “bank” child prepares to trays with two numbers represented with the small decimal cards
The children go and take that quantity of beads on their tray
The children place their small symbol cards on the mat with the corresponding sign.
The “bank” child is now putting everything together. The “bank” child starts counting and when it reaches 10, stops to exchange. The “bank” child will exchange the quantity and continue.
The “bank” child places the large symbol cards on the beads, does the “magic” and places the result on the mat.
Observations for the dynamic addition
The guide will encourage the children to start counting from the ones to avoid returning to exchange.

sections.label: Presentation of changing game for the subtraction

blocks.text: The guide prepares a tray with the thousand cube with the large decimal symbol card
On another tray the guide places only a small decimal symbol card
The guide says that she wants to take away only one bead, but in order to do that she needs to decompose the cube in smaller quantities from which to take the bead
The guide asks the child if he remembers from what was composed the cube, and changes it
Then repeats the question for the hundred golden bead square, and changes it
Again repeats the question for the ten golden bead bar, and changes it
The guide takes the bead away and asks the child to help counting what remained on the tray
The guide asks the child to make the magic and forms the operation on the mat.
Presentation of subtraction (dynamic operation)

6 years old

The memory is the capacity to recall owns mind, knowledge or experiences belonging to the past. We can talk of three stages of the memory: recording, retention and the recalling. The better the recording of the knowledge the better is the retaining the knowledge and the recalling. The quality of the recording depends on the motivation, curiosity and the attention that is being paid. Therefor it is crucial the interest someone has and on the one who evokes that interest. What is being recorded has to come in a sequence with the knowledge already obtained it cannot come as a separate experience, this has to do with the unconscious tendency of the brain to carry on with the previous experiences. Maria Montessori talked about the subconscious as a deposit/storage of impressions that has been absorbed and knowledge that has been acquired. Mario Montessori said that the subconscious can be compared to a room in darkness in which are stored experiences, experiences which the individual has acquired during his life. This room is not arranged in a harmonious way, instead everything is piled up like in a warehouse. The mind seeking a solution is a like the beam of a lighthouse searching until finding it and bring it to the light of the consciousness. All the experiences accumulated even the forgotten ones are the base of the identity of the individual. The construction of the subconscious mind is not
nly having to do with the building of the organism but also with the functioning of
the organism.

1. Same presentation as in the “Snake game in the search for 10” only that now

the children can just recognize the first beads and start from that number counting. The rest stays the same. (E.g. 7, 8, 9, 10 and the child stops) Counting the bead bars isolated two by two 2. Another presentation is to isolate the first two bead bars, recognize the first one and start from there counting the second (E.g. if the first bar is 5 and the second is 7 – the child will count 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12). When done the first two bead bars will replace them with the golden bar and the remainder or only the remainder depending of the case (For the example with the 5 and 7 – the child will place a golden bead bar and a black remainder bar of 2). Then another bead can be isolated from the snake and the counting starts with the remainder bead bar. The process is repeated until the coloured bead snake is finished.

Activity
Passage from the control chart 1 to the control chart 2
The children should have a copy of the control chart 1.
The guide invites the child to look on the control chart 1, on the first column 1+1=2 and asks the child to look if there is another combination equal.

A board with 10 columns and 10 rows – with 100 holes. At the top, over the rows there are numbers written up to 10 in black. In the left top corner, there is round slot for the counter. The green counter is for marking the multiplier. On the left side there is a rectangular slot for the cards from 1 to 10 (multiplicand).
1 box with 100 green beads
1 green counter
9 little cards with the numbers from 1 to 9
Booklet with all the combinations of the multiplication – 10 pages (multiplication
f 1, multiplication of 2, and so on up to 10). All the multiplication keep the first
number constant (multiplicand) and the second one increases (multiplier).
A box with the 100 loose combinations
Control chart 1 – a chart with all the multiplications with the results written in red.
Paper for the child to write his own multiplication
Presentation of the material to the child
The guide shows the board to the child, shows him the holes and how to place the beads
The guide reinforces that there is a special way to place the beads and invites the child to order the cards from 1 to 10 and choose one
The child chooses 8 and the guide shows him how to place the card in the slot for the multiplicand
The guide says that he is going to multiply this number 3 times and shows to the child how to place the green counter over the number 3 which marks the 3rd column
The guide places the beads in columns and invites the child to count after a column is filled.
The guide says “8 times 1 equals 8”, for the next one “8 times 2 equals 16”
At the end, the guide says “8 times 3 equals 24” and writes it down.
Presentation of the multiplication using the booklet
The guide shows the booklet to the child and says that he can find the answers using the board
The guide invites the child to do the first multiplication “1 x 1 = “
The child does the multiplication and reads the result 1
The guide invites the child to write the result on the booklet
The guide invites the child to continue with the next multiplication
When the child finished the first page, the guide shows to the child how to use the control chart 1.
The child reads and the guide confirms for the results
The child cleans the beads from the board and continues with the next page.
Observations for the multiplication using the booklet

If the child is on the page of 4, for example he will do 4 x 1 = 4, write it down in the booklet, move the counter on the top of the number 2 and continue placing beads counting 5, 6, 7, 8. He writes the new product in his booklet, moves the counter on top the number 3 and continue placing the beads and counting 9, 10, 11, 12. He writes down the product in the booklet and continues in the same manner.
Presentation of the multiplication using the loose combinations
The guide shows the box with loose combinations to the child. “Here are all the combinations with which you worked before”
The guide invites the child to choose the first combination and read it 3 x 6 =
The guide invites the child to write it down on its paper
The child does the multiplication with the beads and reads the result 18
The guide invites the child to write the result on the paper
The child removes all the beads from the board and the counter.
The guide invites the child to continue by choosing another multiplication
The guide shows to the child how to use the control chart 1 and lets it up to him when he wants to check his results.
When the child is doing 8 x 4, after he is done we can invite him to try doing 4 x 8. He will be able to observe that the beads on the board form 2 equal rectangles but with a different orientation
Control chart 1
Activity
Passage from the control chart 1 to the control chart 2
The children should have a copy of the control chart 1.
The guide invites the child to look on the control chart 1, on the first column 1x1=2 and asks the child to look if there is another combination equal.
The child cannot find another.
The guide passes to the next one 1x2 = 2, looks for another combination with the product 2, finds 2x1 = 2 and cancels with a line the 2x1 = 2
The guide passes to the next one 1x3 = 3 and cancels the 3x1=4
The guide continues until all the repeated combinations are canceled.
In this manner, 45 combinations are eliminated. So now, there are left 55 combinations, which are strictly necessary for the memorization of the multiplication.
If we align the results of the combinations, we will get the control chart 2.
Originally this table ended up at 9, as these are all the essential multiplication. Maria Montessori added also the 10 to have all the numbers from the decimal system.
In the chart 2 for addition the diagonal was made of the doubles and now for multiplication the diagonal is made of the square of the numbers.
Help the children memorize all the results and combinations for the multiplication
Help the children understand the commutative propriety of the multiplication
Preparation for the squaring

Observations for working with the chart 3

When the child will have to check his operation, he might not find the exact combination (E.g. 3x2) so he will have to look for the product of the combination 2x3 applying the commutative property of the multiplication.
Activity
Passage from the chart 3 to the chart 4
The children should have a copy of the chart 3.
If before in the activity “Passage from the chart 1 to chart 2” we eliminated 45 multiplications from the control chart 1, now we are going to eliminate 45 results.

After the elimination, we end up with the chart 4.

We are very used to thinking of division as of the opposite of multiplication but what’s interesting is that we can start working with division using an approach which is very different from multiplication.
The children worked before with the decimal system material and the stamp game doing division but if the child has to divide mentally in the future, he has to remember the division facts.
When it comes to the memorization of division the highest dividend is 81, the highest divisor is 9 and the highest quotient is 9. These kind of divisions we can call them little divisions.

A board with 9 columns and 9 rows – with 81 holes. At the top, over the columns, there are numbers written up to 9 in black on a green background and rows are also numbered up to 9. In the left top corner, there is a green circle with the number 1 written.
9 green skittles
1 box with 81 green beads
1 green counter
Booklet with all the combinations of the division – 36 pages
Chart 1 – a chart with all the necessary divisions.
Paper for the child to write his own divisions
Presentation of the material to the child
The guide shows the board to the child, shows him the holes, how to place the beads and the lid of the green beads face up next to the box.
The guide invites the child to choose a number up to 81
The child choses 10 and the guide invites him to divide by 2
The guide puts in the lid 10 green beads
The guide takes 2 skittle and positions them on the green strip
The guide shares the beads to the 2 green skittles
The guide shows the child how to read the result by counting the beads that
ne skittle receives or by looking at the number of the row on the left side.
The guide invites the child to do a division by himself.
The guide talks with the child about the limits of the “game” – we can give only 9 to a skittle and we can use only 9 skittle.
The guide continues to explain that another rule is that what we have left as a remainder in the tray cannot be equal or higher that the answer

The guide later can introduce the child with the correct names: the number that we divide is called “the dividend”, to how many we divide is called “the devisor”, the result that one gets is “the quotient” and what’s left is the “the remainder”.
Presentation of “Finding the relevant dividends”
The guide starts inviting the child to use the terms for division
The guide reads with the child the heading of the form (dividend, divisor, quotient, remainder) and explains the terms
The guide introduces the two rules for this activity: the quotient cannot be higher than 9 and the remainder is never equal or greater than the divisor.
The guide will start with the highest dividend for working: 81 and invites the child to write 81 in the booklet
The guide invites the child to work with all the 81 beads in the box and to place the 9 skittles at top to do the division: “81 : 9 =”
The child does the division and reads the result 9
The guide shows to the child that nothing is left in the tray and says that this is a special division it is called “exact”
The guide invites the child to use red to underline in red the dividend
Continue by dividing with 8 skittles.
The guide says that it is not necessary to remove all the beads, the guide removes the skittle for 9 and the beads for it – he invites the child to redistribute all the beads from the box
The guide invites the child to read the result and the remainder beads in the lid
The child says that the result is 9 and remainder 9
The guide says that this division doesn’t follow the rules of the game and crosses it in the form
The guide says invites the child to do the same for “81 : 8 = ”
The guide invites the child to write the division on the booklet but because again it doesn’t follow the rules the child crosses it
The guide invites him to try with 80
The child clears the board, takes a new form, and writes 80 for the heading.
The child makes sure that he has now 80 beads in the box
The guide says that again we will try to divide to 9.
The child places the beads and reads the result 80:9 = 8 r 16
The child writes it down but crosses it
The guide invites him to try 80 : 8
The child places the beads and reads the result 80 : 8 = 9 r 8
The guide asks the child if the division follows the rules and because the remainder is equal with the divisor they cancel this one again
The guide lets the child try also 80: 7 and the child will understand that this is not good as well so he will have to cross it again
The guide invites the child to go to the next number and write it down on the next form “79”
The child clears the board, takes a new form, and writes 79 for the heading.
The child makes sure that he has now 79 beads in the box
The guide says that again we will try to divide to 9.
The child places the beads and reads the result 79:9 = 8 r 7
The child writes it down in his form as this division follows the rules
The guide invites him to try 79 : 8
The child places the beads and reads the result 79 : 8 = 9 r 7
The child writes it down in his form as this division follows the rules
The guide invites him to try 79 : 7
The child places the beads and reads the result 79 : 7 = 9 r 16
The guide asks the child if the division follows the rules and because the rest is higher than the divisor they cancel this one again
The guide can discuss with the child that once one division breaks our rules we can move to the next form with the new dividend.
The child will take a new form and try again for the dividend for 78, 77, 76, 75, 74, 73
When the child reaches the form of 72 he will observe that there are two “special” divisions with the remainder of 0 which he has to underline in red.
The child will continue independently until reaching “1 : 1 = 1”
The guide will invite the child to look for the forms with the dividend underlined in red
The child will find 36 forms and these are the ones that make the booklet for division
Observations for “Finding the relevant dividends”
At the end of the work (after 81 forms) the child would have found 120 combinations with remainder and 81 combinations without remainder, a total
f 201 combinations
Presentation of the division using the booklet
The guide shows the booklet to the child and says that he can find the answers using the board
The guide invites the child to do the first multiplication “81 :9 = “
The child does the division and reads the result 9
The guide invites the child to write the result on the booklet
The guide invites the child to continue with the next division
When the child finished the first page, the guide shows to the child how to use the chart 1.
The child reads and the guide confirms for the results
The child cleans the beads from the board and continues with the next page.
Presentation of how to use the chart 1 for the control of the results
When the child has to check with the chart 1 he has to put one finger on the dividend and the second finger on the divisor.

For example to check the 36 : 9, the child will have to place the first finger on the column of 36 on the top row and the second finger on the row for :9. The first finger goes down on the column and the second finger continues to right
n the row until the finger meet and the child reads the result 4

For the next division 36 : 8, the child will have to place the first finger on the column of 36 on the top row and the second finger on the row for :8. The first finger goes down on the column and the second finger continues to right on the row until the finger meet but this time there is no result in the square. The child has to continue with the finger to the right on the same row until reaching a result. In this case it will be 4. The child writes it down and it looks to which column it corresponds to the column of 32 so the operation will have as a remainder the difference between 36 and 32 – in our case 4. The child writes down remainder 4. “36 :8 = 4 r 4”
Observation for finding the dividends from division chart 1 in the multiplication chart 4
If we use the multiplication chart 4 and cancel the row of 10
Then we can continue to cancel all the repeated numbers.
We are left with all the dividends from the division chart 1

children.title: Group five: Passage to abstraction “The hierarchies”

blocks.text: Maria Montessori called this group “The hierarchies”, as now the children will work with the material and the pen and on the paper with the goal to make a passage towards working only with the pen on the paper. She said that you cannot work well on paper with abstract concepts if you don’t respect the hierarchies. The material can be presented once the child has clearly the concepts and his memorization facts. For example for the addition the child must have clear the concept of addition and have memorized the facts for addition.

The “Story of the numbers” is one of the last cosmic fables that are told in elementary. It is told after the story of the Ox and the House. They might come in a fairy tale form but they are stories of truth. The Cosmic fables open the study areas; in this case, the “Story of the numbers” opens the area of arithmetic.

Presentation of the cosmic fable “Story of the numbers”
Tell the story

Today we have a new story, but before I begin with this new story, do you remember the story of the ox and the house, the story that we can think now as the story of the alphabet. Let us think of that story. With that story, we learned how the people found a new silent way to communicate, talk to each other. The story of the ox was about the written language, about how the people first spoke and wrote and about how the people first listened and read. Today we want to think of some particular words and their specific signs. Do we have words answering to questions such as: “How many?” or “How long?”. Well if we think of our day to day, we might ask ourselves: “How many oranges I need to last me all the week?” Of course, the people a long time ago, they did not have supermarkets to buy their food, they had to go out and find their food. They had to gather plants, hunt animals and not only that they had names for the different plants or animals, we think that they also had words for answering questions like “How many?”. So let us imagine that times. Imagine that the people came back from a hunt and they wanted to tell the
ther people how many animals they saw, or how many bushes with berries
they saw or how many bushes they picked and how many were left for others.

Let us think that they had to travel so they had to ask themselves how many days it will take until finding water again. When we answer all these questions, what do we use? – Yes, we use numbers All the human groups had at least a few words of this kind. We have not found any human group that does not have at least a few words for numbers. It is true that there were some groups that had only a few number words, for example, some had only one, two, three and then the word “many”. What about us – what do we have after three – the guide counts. If they had only a few numbers maybe they did not required too many numbers. There is a record of a human group had only “one” and “many” and the name for “one” was “alone”. We think that the human beings used words for numbers first in a spoken form and only later, they wrote them as signs or numbers. Let us think of that time when these signs for numbers came into being: we can imagine the human beings speaking, and using gestures. What part of the body is handy when we think of the numbers: yes – the hand/ the fingers. We can imagine a man long ago trying to tell his people how many animals he saw – he used his fingers to remember and tell the others how many antelopes he saw. He could use stones or sticks to remember how many animals he saw as well.
[Show chart 1: Stones- Malayan method]

The Malayans used stones to remember how many things they saw. In some parts of the world this method was used by shepherds – they had bags with little stones – one for each sheep they had. As each sheep came into the pen, they took out a stone, if the bag was empty it meant that he had all the sheep. The number of stones corresponded to all the sheep (Note: this is one to one correspondence). The stones did not have any special signs it was just one stone for each animal
The Sumerians lived in the Mesopotamia, and you remember how they used to make tablets from clay for writing, they used styluses to make marks in the
tables. They had so many tablets that we can think of the tablets as collections. They made some special marks on the tablets. [Show chart 2: Sumerian number system]

Look at this one, this one is for 1, this for 4 and this one for 5 – it is like the stone counting. Now look at 10, a completely new mark – they did not repeat the marks used before. This sign represents a grouping of 10.

If this is 10 and this is 1 – what do you think this one represents (pointing at 38) Now let us look at this one – it looks like one but represents 60. We have to be careful to know when we have 1 or 60. These signs are for 600.

While the Sumerians were developing this system, the Egyptians were developing their own number system. Egyptians like the Sumerians were farmers. The Egyptians unlike the Sumerians were unified under a king, which they though as a god, they called him a pharaoh. During this time because they were so many under the king, they had many things to carve on the stone
r print on papyrus. Do you remember their special signs? – the hieroglyphs.
These are their special hieroglyphs for numbers.
[Show chart 3: Egyptian number system]

They had one for 1, than they had to put up to 9 of them for the number 9 but for the number 10 they grouped them under a new sign – that looks like this. After they counted from 10 to 90, they got to another one for 100. Let us look at all of them for a few minutes and let us guess the number that they wrote here.
We heard before about the Greeks other ancient civilization. They had 2 systems to write – this one is the old one.
[Show chart 4: Greek number system]

How do you think that they wrote 2, 3 or 4. Now let us look at 5 – we heard this number before, “Pente”, in Pentagon. The Greeks instead of saying “Pe” for P they said “Pi” – look at this first letter in Greek for “Pi” and how the sign for 5 looked. Let us think of how they would write 6 and 7. Let us look at how the Greeks wrote 10 – they called it “Deka” as this is how they said 10 in their language. For 100, in Greek they said Hekaton, and this one is the sign for 100.

For 1000, in Greek they said Chilioi, and this one is the sign for 1000. For 10000, in Greek they said Myrioi, and this one is the sign for 10 000. Let us look at the number here – can we decode this number (optional with the children)
The ancient romans had their own way of writing the numbers and you might have seen them before. Where have you seen the roman numerals?
[Show chart 5: Roman number system]

We see these signs in many places, movies, clocks, in books or to indicate the years on plaques. Not everyone agrees of how these signs came into existence, now we will explore what some of the people think and we will came back to it in the future. The sign for 1 has like little feet, and it was repeated for 2, 3 or 4 and here it is the sign for 5. For the number 4 they did like this IIII like adding, but if you represent it like this IV, it means ”one less than 5”, like a subtraction. The 5 might reminds us of the peace sign or the letter “V”. Some people think it was for this separation in the hand. If we know the sign for 5 and 1 we can make the rest up to 9. You remember how we made 4 in a different way, a more economical
ne. Look like this IX (can remember us of 10-1). The sign for 10 can represent

two hands making the signs for 5. Can you imagine how to write 49? For the number 50 we have this sign that looks like L, and for 100 we have C. The say 100 in Latin it is Centum and if we draw the C with hard corners and cut in half we will get our L for 50. Let us look at the signs for 500 and 1000. In Latin 1000 is Mille, so they wrote an M. The romans might have wrote the M in a more cursive way and the half of it is the D that we can see here. (Note: The children can explore the rest) Now if we look at this number, then we can decode it, right?
[Place all the charts face up with the exception of Chart 1]
Let us have a good look at these charts. The Sumerians came from Mesopotamia/Asia (close to Europe), Egyptians from Africa, the Greeks from Europe, and the romans from Europe.
[Show chart 6: Chinese number system]

Let us look at these ones from China, who are coming from very far away if we compare them with the others. Let us have a look at 1, 2, 3 – they look familiar but the other look different. So far, with all the signs apart of the 1, 2, 3 we haven’t seen anything like these numbers.
We didn’t get our numbers from the Sumerians, Egyptians, Greek, romans or Chinese – where did we get them from? From the people in India.

To understand this we have to go back to a long time ago, more than 1300 years ago in India. In the 7th century, a new religion came into the world and spread very fast, the Islam. After the death of their prophet, Mohamed, the religion spread as the Arabs conquered many parts of the world. The conquest went from the Atlantic in the West right over to India in the East and from North Africa right into Spain. Not only that they were great conquerors but they were also great traders. They traded from India all the way to Spain. They became a kind of bridge between the East and the West. There were caravans moving from India all the way to Spain, and the knowledge traveled and traveled with those caravans. These Arabs who were conquerors and traders they became madly passionate about learning. So true, that they developed a great center of learning in a city which was called Madinat al Salaam – “the city of peace”, now it is called Bagdad. This location appears also in many stories from “1001 nights”. Because the Arab empire was so huge, then different parts were ruled by different people and the rulers were called: Caliphs (leader of the faithful). One caliph lived in the city of Bagdad and he created a big library for himself, so large,

that it became a library for everyone. In this city, there was also the biggest book market in the world, with many manuscripts in many languages and many translators to translate everything in Arabic. This library was called the House of Wisdom and the manuscripts were translated from Latin, Coptic and Greek. In this way, the Arab world absorbed a wealth of knowledge in its tradition. One day in 1733 AD there was a caravan that came all the way from India and entered the city of Bagdad. The caravan brought gifts, and among these gifts, there was a special book that was immediately translated into Arabic. In this book, there were these signs from India, the numbers from which we take our numbers signs.
[Show chart 7: Old European numerals]
If we want to think of how these numbers were pronounced we can look at the
ther chart from Sanskrit. This book coming from India also had the zero in it.

The Indian word for 0 was “sunya” (pronounced shunia) and it meant empty. This Indian word: “empty”, was translated into Arabic and became “sifr”. Later in Latin became “zephyrum”, then “zephiro” in Italian and in English, we got to call it “zero”. Once the Arabs had these Indian numbers, they took them everywhere including to Spain and this is how we got them.
[Show chart 8: From the Hindu to the European number system]

We took our numbers from the Arabs, so we tend to call them Arab numbers or numerals but it would be fairer to call them Hindu-Arab numerals. How many symbols do we need to write all our numbers? Ten signs – it is not a lot of signs to be able to write an infinite number of numbers. With these ten signs I can write numbers as big as 10, 100, 1000, 10 000, 100 000, 1 000 000 or 1 000 000 000 000 000. The zero is the one that helps us to make so easily big numbers. It took a lot of time to bring the zero; it was no use for them at the beginning to have a number for empty/nothing. Now, we can ask
urselves then why the Indians needed the zero?

In Europe, the Europeans took a long time to accept these numbers, as they liked their own roman numbers as impractical as they were. After some time they changed their mind and understood the power of 0 and this helped the mathematics – opening so many doors for the usage of the numbers.

Notes on the story
The Sumerians used the same sign for 1 and 60 and they sometimes used a placeholder not to get confused.
To calculate comes from the Latin word for “pebble”.
The arithmetical operations with any other number system is challenging, the scholars in that times didn’t use their numerical systems for arithmetical
perations, which would be carried out in a concrete fashion, instead they
used them only for recording the answers.
Important points of the “Story of the Numbers”
Every human group had some idea of number systems, it doesn’t how developed or primitive these were – it shows the importance of a number system in the daily
Human groups with reduced number systems
Siriono – from Bolivia
Yanomamo – from Brazil

Bacairi – from Brazil
The importance of grouping for creating an efficient number system
The most important bases found in the number systems are (5, 10, 20) – as it corresponds to the human fingers and toes.
The importance of the notation as a way to facilitate the use of the number system. Complicated signs or repetitive signs make the number system hard to use.

Sumerian’s writing was called cuneiform (from the wedge shaped writing from Latin cuneus for “wedge”)
The Greek numeric system it is called acrophonic (initial letter)
The recent system of the Greeks was the alphabetic one

To arouse the children’s interest in the numbers. It helps them understand how the number system that we use is so easy compared with the previous ones.
To help the children develop of a sense of appreciation for the work of the humans that came before us.
6-12 years old

The material is concrete material to show the children the importance of the hierarchies. The wooden hierarchical material is a continuation of the golden bead material, which was limited at 1000. The wooden hierarchical material shows clearly the family grouping.
Big green cube representing 1 million
Red prism representing 100 thousand
Blue bar representing 10 thousand
Small green cube representing thousand
Small red prism representing 1 hundred
Small blue bar representing 10
Tiny green cube representing 1 (side of 0.5 cm)

The numbers are centered
The cards are white with text in black
The families are marked with spaces

children.title: Concept of group division with the Stamp game

blocks.text: The previous division done with the stamp game was distributive division. The answer was “how many one unit received”. For the group division the answer is going to be “how many groups have we formed”.

For the group division we are trying to form groups of as many units as the divisor, the number of groups formed is going to be the quotient and the remainder is what we couldn’t use to form a group – in other words the rest is always smaller than the divisor.
4 small bowls with small wood blocks/squares made of wood for 1, 10, 100, 1000 with the numbers written on the wood.
A box with 9 green skittles, 9 blue skittles, 9 red skittles, 1 large green skittle and 1 green, 1 blue and 1 red counters (placeholders)
4 little dishes
1 box with:
1 long white stripe
6 orange place holders
White blank squares of paper
Orange blank squares of paper
White cards with the numbers from 0 – 9 in black
Presentation of the concept for Children’s House
The guide invites the child to divide 1958 : 636 = in the distributive way.
After the child is done, the guide says that he is going to show the child a different way to divide by looking at how many groups of 636 he can form.
The child prepares the quantity to be divided
The guide places the skittles for 636, but this time the skittles stay close together.
The guide forms one time 636 from the dividend stamps
The guide repeats until he has formed three times the group 636, every time with a gap in between the groups
The guide checks the remainder and makes sure it cannot form another group from it.
The guide says that the answer is the number of groups formed: 3
The guide says that the remainder is 60 and writes down 1958 : 636 = 3 r60
Presentation of the concept for Elementary
The guide says to the child that now the skittles do not represent themselves but they know represent a group.
The guide invites the child to divide “12: 3 =” in the distributive way.
The guide invites the child to do it in a different way. Now the three skittle will represent a group – “a group of three”.
Now that the skittles are a group of three the guide says it is going to form groups equals to the divisor.
The guide forms 4 groups of 3.
The guide says that the answer for our division is “how many group we have
btained”.
The guide writes down the answer.
The guide compares the answer with the previous one obtained by the child, and they conclude that are the same.
Presentation of the short division
The guide uses the stamps to form the dividend
The guide uses the white blank squares to write the divisor and places it on the left of the white line
The orange circles are placeholders for the digits of the answer (quotient)
The orange blank squares are to write the remainder
The guide writes on a strip of paper 465 : 4 = and place it on top of the white stripe
The guide forms the dividend with the stamps under the white stripe
The guide writes on a white square paper the divisor: 4
The guide moves down the tiles of the hundreds
The guide says let’s find out how many groups of 4 hundreds can we make.
The guide places one orange placeholder over the white stripe on top of the hundreds
The guide looks how many groups of 4 hundreds he made, it is only 1, so it places one counter with the number 1 over the orange placeholder.
The guide passes to the next inferior hierarchy.
The guide places the orange placeholder over the white stripe for the tens.
The guide looks how many groups of 4 tens he can make from the 6 tiles of tens.
The guide forms 1 group, slides the tiles at the level of the ones of the hundreds, but there are still 2 tiles left that cannot be included in the group
So the guide places on top of the orange placeholder the card with the number 1
The guide passes to the next inferior hierarchy.

The guide places the orange placeholder for on top of the white stripe for the units and looks how many groups of 4 units he can make from the 5 tile for units but also from the 2 tens tile which could not be part of group before.
The guide makes 6 groups of 4 units tiles and there is still one unit tile left.
The guide places card with the number 6 over the orange placeholder.
The guide write on an orange square paper the remainder of 1.
The guide writes down the answer on the paper slip 116 r1
Presentation of the long division
Two digits in the divisor
The guide writes on a strip of paper 3936: 32 = and place it on top of the white strip of paper
The guide forms the dividend with the stamps under the white strip
The guide writes on a white square paper the divisor: 32
The guide moves down the tiles of the thousands and hundreds and places
ne orange placeholder over the white stripe on top the hundreds. As we are
making groups of hundreds.
The guide places looks how many groups of 32 hundreds he could make. It is possible to make only 1 so it places one card with the number 1 over the
range placeholder.
There are left 7 tiles of hundreds which are not part of the groups formed.
The guide passes to the next inferior hierarchies.
The guide brings down the tiles for the hundreds and the tens.
The guide places the orange placeholder over the white stripe over the tens.
The guide looks how many groups of 32 tens he can make from the 7 tiles of hundreds and 3 tiles of tens.

The guide forms 2 groups with the necessary exchanges, slides the tiles at the level of the ones of the thousands and hundreds from before, but there are still 9 tiles of tens left that cannot be included in a group before.
So the guide places on top of the orange placeholder the card with the number 2.
The guide passes to the next inferior hierarchies.

The guide places the orange placeholder over the units and looks how many groups of 32 units he can make from the 6 tiles for the units but also 9 tiles for the tens which could not be part of group before.
The guide makes 3 groups of 32 from the tens and units tiles
The guide places the card with the number 3 over the orange placeholder.
The guide writes down the answer on the paper slip 123. There is no remainder this time. Three digits in the divisor

The guide forms the dividend with the stamps under the white strip
The guide writes on a white square paper the divisor: 245
The guide moves down the tiles of the thousand, hundreds, tens and places
ne orange placeholder over the white stripe in the place of the tens (the last
hierarchy).
The guide looks how many groups of 245 tens he could make. It is possible to make 2 groups, so it places one card with the number 2 over the orange placeholder.
There are left 7 tiles of hundreds and 4 tiles of tens.
The guide passes to the next inferior hierarchies.
The guide brings down the tiles for the hundreds, the tens and the units.
The guide places the orange placeholder over the white stripe over the units.

The guide forms 3 groups with the necessary exchanges, but there is still 1 tile

f the hundreds and the board of tens these three situations can occur:
Board of hundreds has more groups than the board of tens
The child with the board of the hundreds can help the one with the tens to agree to a number of groups
Board of hundreds has less groups than the board of tens
The child with the board of the tens removes the extra groups so that his board will agree with the board of the hundreds
Board of hundreds has the same number of groups as the board of tens
The division continues and the board of units will try to match the number of groups on the boards of tens and hundreds. If it can than they will have to agree for a group less.

It resembles the sensorial decanomial only that now the squares and the rectangles are not colour coded and they have inscriptions with the products that they represent.
10 folders numbered from 0 to 9
Folder 0: 10 dark blue squares with the product written in the middle and in the top left corner with the number and the power (E.g. 100 in the center and 102 in the top left corner)

Folder 1: 18 rectangles with one side of 1 and the other side variable. These rectangles represent all the multiplications where the multiplicand is 1. 1x1 is missing because it is already in the “Folder 0”

Folder 2: 16 rectangles with one side of 2 and the other side variable. These rectangles represent all the multiplications where the multiplicand is 2. 2x2 is missing because it is already in the “Folder 0” – 1x2 and 2x1 are missing as these are in “Folder 1”

Folder 3: 14 rectangles with one side of 3 and the other side variable. These rectangles represent all the multiplications where the multiplicand is 2. 2x2 is missing because it is already in the “Folder 0” – 1x2 and 2x1 are missing as these are in “Folder 1”

Folder 4: 12 rectangles with the height of 4 and the other side variable. These rectangles represent all the multiplications where the multiplicand is 4. 2x2 is missing because it is already in the “Folder 0” – 1x2 and 2x1 are missing as these are in “Folder 1” and so on

Folder 5: 10 rectangles with the height of 5 and the other side variable. These rectangles represent all the multiplications where the multiplicand is 5 except the ones already present in previous folders.

Folder 6: 8 rectangles with the height of 6 and the other side variable. These rectangles represent all the multiplications where the multiplicand is 6 except the ones already present in previous folders.

Folder 7: 6 rectangles with the height of 7 and the other side variable. These rectangles represent all the multiplications where the multiplicand is 7 except the ones already present in previous folders.

Folder 8: 4 rectangles with the height of 8 and the other side variable. These rectangles represent all the multiplications where the multiplicand is 8 except the ones already present in previous folders.

Folder 9: 2 rectangles with the height of 9 and the other side variable. These rectangles represent all the multiplications where the multiplicand is 9 except the ones already present in previous folders.

The multiplication is the opposite arithmetic operation of the division; it is used to the extent that to check a division we use always the multiplication. By the time, the child gets to this work he needs to have memorized the multiplication facts. This work does not have the aim of memorization of the multiplication. A multiple is a number that contains another number perfectly. 25 is the multiple of 5. The multiple of a number can be obtained by multiplying that number by all the natural numbers. As the natural numbers are infinite, so the multiple numbers are infinite.

Find the LCM of the three numbers
The guide says “With these prime factors, can we find the lowest common multiple (LCM)?”
The guide invites the child to refresh himself the concept of the lowest common multiple.
The guide asks the child if “the LCM is going to be a small number or a big?” Check how many times each prime factor is repeated in the three numbers and add it to LCM
The guide says “Let’s look for the 2, we have it once in our first number and twice in the second and no 2 in the third”
The guide says “We are going to write it the highest number of times as it repeats in one number. We found it repeated it twice in the 12 so we write” – “LCM = 2 x 2”
The guide says “Let’s look for the 3, we have it once in our first number and
nce in the second and once in the third.”
The guide says “We are going to write it the highest number of times as it repeats in one number, let’s add it to our LCM” – “LCM = 2 x 2 x 3”
The guide says, “Let’s look for the 5, we have it once in our first number and don’t have it in the second and we don’t have it in the third.”
The guide says “We are going to write it the highest number of times as it repeats in one number, let’s add it to our LCM” – “LCM = 2 x 2 x 3 x 5”
The guide says, “Let’s look for the 7, we don’t have it in our first number, don’t have it in the second and we have it in the third number once.”
The guide says “We are going to write it as the highest number of times that is repeated in one number, let’s add it to our LCM” – “LCM = 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 x 7”
The guide says “Let’s calculate our LCM” – “LCM = 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 420”

The guide invites the child how many rectangles have to be repeated in order to reach 30 placed on their side of 10 cm. The answer is “30 : 10 = 3”
The guide invites the child to calculate how many rectangles are required in total “5 x 3 = 15”. We need a total of 15 squares.
Problem 2

Read the problem, find the GCF and use it to solve the problem Problem: “We have a garden with the sides of 60, 72, 48 and 36. We plant a tree in each corner and we want to plant trees in between but the trees have to be at the same distance on all the sides, but we want to be the longest distance possible in between the trees. How many trees do we need to buy?”

ther.

The guide invites the child to sum the results and find the total number of trees required

6-9 years old

In our bead material, we find represented as concrete material, the powers from 1 to 3 of the first ten numbers (1-10) – bead bars, bead squares and bead cubes. A bead bar is the base to the first power. The squares represent the number at the second power. Repeating a square, as many times as there are units in the base, we obtain the cube. The cubes represent the number at the third power. While working with the cabinet the children will find that, there is another power in the cabinet, the power zero.
Psychoarithmetic, note 17 (Italian version)

“It is necessary to help the children understand the numeral structures created artificially by the human beings around numbers. The numbers are governed by a rule that consists of obeying the law proper to the group. Each number is made by single units, so 4 is made up of 4 elements and as soon as the elements organize themselves in groups they obey the law of the group.”

The bead bar is made from the single units, but as soon as they are together that bead bar obey the rules of the number of that they represent. A power is the product of the base times itself, as many times as desired.
