blocks.text: Slips with story problems
Presentation of the story problems
Problem 1 – “The story of the princess Lilivati”

“An Indian princess lived in a beautiful palace which had a wonderful garden. This garden had different kinds of flowerbeds and a fountain in the middle. Lilivati went in the garden to play. She gets a pearl necklace as a gift from her father. She puts on the necklace and goes to play in the garden. While playing the pearls of the necklace scatter in the garden. Lilivati sits on the border of the fountain. The animals in the garden decide to help the princess. The frogs, ants, rabbits and the birds all help to find the pearls. 1/2 was brought by the frogs, 1/4 by the ants, 1/8 by the rabbits and the rest by the birds. How much of the pearls in fractions has been brought by the birds?”
Notes for the problem:
The children can use the divided circles material and find out the answer (A:
The birds brought 1/8)
Problem 2 – “A very thirsty man”

“A man has a glass of wine, the man drinks 1/3 of the glass of wine and then refills the glass with water. Now he drinks a half of the mixture and he adds to the remainder enough water to refill the glass. Them he drinks 2/3 and refills the glass with the water. How much wine and how much water remained in the glass?“
Notes for the problem:
The guide places the frame and the whole inset representing the full glass of wine.
When the man drinks 1/3 the guide replaces the whole with 3/3 and takes away 1/3 away
To get the idea of the wine mixed with the water the guide places the thirds
pposite to each other
To represent that he drank half the guide removes the 1/3 piece.
To represent that he drank 2/3 of the mixture, the guide exchanges the 1/3 with 3/9 and arranges them opposite to each other. The guide removes 2/9 to represent that the man drank 2/3 of the content.
The answers at the question are 1/9 of wine and 8/9 of water.
The guide can invite the child to write down the operations from the problem.
Problem 3 – “Julia and the sweets”

“One Sunday Julia receives a package of sweets. The mother says that the sweets have to be divided in 7 parts and she is allowed to drink only a 1/7 per day. On Sunday manages to abide by the daily ratio, but on Monday she eats also the sweets for the Tuesday. What fraction of the sweets remains for the rest
f the week? “
Notes for the problem:
The children can use the divided circles material and find out the answer and also by writing down(A: 4/7)
Problem 4 – “Finding the height of the rectangle”
“We have a rectangle with the base 2 meters and it is 2/3 of the height. What is the height of our rectangle? “ Notes for the problem:
The children can use the divided circles material and find out the answer and also by writing down(A: 3 meters)
Problem 5 – “Finding the height of the pole”
“We have a pole and we know that 5/6 of the height is 10m. What is the height
f our pole? “
Notes for the problem:
The children can use the divided circles material and find out the answer and also by writing down (A: 12 meters)
To help the children understand division with fractions and discover by themselves the rule for the division.
6-9 years old
A decimal number is a fraction of the unit, but it is a special fraction. In case of the decimal numbers, the denominator is either 10 or a power of 10.

Another special thing about decimal fractions is that there are different ways of writing, with fraction notations or represented by standard decimal number notations. The decimal number notation has a dot that separates the whole number part from the decimal number part.

Introduction of the snake game and introduction of the concepts: positive & negative
The guide talks to the child about how we see the negative numbers with the temperature, altitude, etc.

The guide says that the negative numbers came into being very late. Up to 1500, negative numbers were not considered normal numbers, they were called “absurd numbers”. In 1600 there were to be found for the first time identified as negative numbers.
The guide reviews with the children what they already know about the negative numbers – that they have a minus in front
The guide says that today we are going to do a new snake game. In this game the colour bead bars are going to be the positive numbers and we will think of them with a “+” sign in front of them.
The guide says that the grey ones are going to be the negative numbers and will come with the sign of minus.
The guide says that the golden bead bars and the black and white bead bars are going to be positive numbers, therefore with a sign “+”
Prepare the lids, B&W beads, the snake and read it
The guide places the B&W bead bars in a stair.
The guide places two collection lids for the grey and colour bead bars.

The guide says that this time we can think of this snake as an addition snake. It might seem strange but with the bead bars having signs we can do it as an addition. Now I am going to read it and always say the sign of each bead bar.
The guide prepares two empty lids on the lower side under the snake
The guide says “+9 plus -7 plus +5 plus +2 plus -7 plus -1 plus +4 plus +3 plus -6”
Another way of reading the snake: “ positive 9 plus negative 7 plus positive 5 plus positive 2 plus negative 7 plus negative 1 plus positive 4 plus positive 3 plus negative 6”
Do the snake by adding two bead bars at a time
The guide takes the first two bead bars (+9 and - 7)

The guide looks at the bead bars, he says “positive 9 plus negative 7”, one is positive and the other is negative so he says that it is like a subtraction, we can look at the result and we can say “positive 2” and places a B&W bead bar of 2 back in the snake
The guide places the grey bead bar in one lid and the colour bead bars in the
ther lid.

The guide places the B&W bead bar back in the B&W stair and the colour bead bars in the other lid.
The guide continues in the same manner with the rest of the bars from the snake.
Arrange the grey and colour bead bars and check the snake
The guide takes all the grey bead bars and the colour bead bars and
rders them from the longest to the shortest with the grey on the left
side

The guide takes the first grey bead bar of 7 and does the exchanges from the colour bead bars to have a colour bead bar 7. The guide continues by saying the negative 7 cancels the positive 7, their result is zero.
The guide continues in the same manner until all the grey bead bars have an equal pair and the last bead bar of B&W of 2 is matched with a colour bead bar of 2

Blue: cube of hundreds – value of millions
Red: cube of tens – value of thousands
White: cube of units – value of units
24 prisms:

Story of the “Three kings” and placement of the pieces of the trinomial cube
The guide says that we have another cube for the work with the hierarchies but before getting to work with the hierarchical cube I have to tell you a story

Part 1: “The story of the three kings – The characters”. Three kings reign in three different countries, each king in its own borders. The largest and most important kingdom is the kingdom of light ruled by king Sun. The smallest is the kingdom
f the snows and its King is the King White. The third country of intermediate

importance is the Kingdom of air – and its king it is King Blue. Here are our three kings: Sun, Blue and White. All of them are represented by cubes whose size decreases to indicate the different importance of each. The kings are very good friends and one beautiful day they decide to go to a splendid festival
rganized in their honor in a large city of another country.

Part 2: “The procession”. The procession is formed, each king has the same following to that of his friend: 3 nobleman, 3 horseman and 2 bodyguards. It is a beautiful procession. King Sun leads the procession, as he is the most important of all. He is wrapped in an orange cloak. Flanking him to escort him are two guards who are lean but tall, tall as he is. Their uniform is all black. Three nobleman follow them. The noblemen are as tall as their king is, and only a part
f their clothes has the same colour as the King Sun – the rest is black. Long

time it was possible to distinguish people by their clothes. The three horsemen follow, their clothes are also orange and black. In the second place, we find the king Blue. King Blue it is a little smaller and less imposing than his friend that leads the procession. He has also two bodyguards – tall as he is and dressed in black. Three nobleman and three horsemen follow him – having part of their clothes blue and black. In the back the smallest of all it is the King White, he has two bodyguards as tall as him and it is followed by three nobleman and
three horsemen in white and black clothes. The procession continues but the city where they are going it is still far

Part 3: “The battle”. Towards the evening, a fight breaks out. King Sun and King White unite against king Blue. Suddenly from two sides they fall on King Blue and his escorts. A real battle ensues. King Blue defends himself vigorously. The blue noblemen attack the orange horsemen and stand on them removing their insignia. The blue horsemen are reached by the nobleman of the king white and become prisoners stripped of their insignia. The blue king it is surrounded by the guards – his own bodyguards trait him and now he is surrounded by six bodyguards of his own height. King White has moved to the end of the procession, as he fears a sudden attack given the situation. King Sun, his noblemen, and the white horsemen they did not even move as their intervention was not even necessary. Now that the fight it is over and the dust it is settled we can look at this procession that restarts its march. The central part it is occupied by six bodyguards who lead the blue king to prison in his blue cloak. When the game is over they free him – it was all a game and not a real fight, part of the parade to entertain the public. Everyone is freed and continue in this exact order to cross now in the territory of the decimal system. The end.

This chapter comes after squaring, but the children do not need to have done all the work with squaring before starting this chapter as well. These two chapters go in parallel. Extracting the square root it is the inverse operation of squaring – it is a special division where the divisor and the quotient are the same.

The age depends on their knowledge but this work should start around the age of 8. By the time, they finished working with the square they should be working abstractly. The root in the presentation of the concept it contains only 1 digit.

Exclude the last digit

Annex the new root digit to the diviser and multiply it by the new root digit and subtract the product from the number originally available.
Annex the next group to the result of the subtraction

Measurement involves the process of comparing and counting. It is a process of finding how many measuring units are contained in a certain thing. To have a unit of measurement it helps the people to communicate by having a common unit to compare. The humans have invented different measurement units depending of what they are measuring: distance, time, mass, force and so on.
To successfully communicate the measurement, the humans have to make sure that they are using the correct measuring device and language.

Measurement activities are very meaningful for the children as it gives to the children a clearer way to relate to the environment and everything that surrounds them. It helps the children with their tendency to be exact.
With practice the human beings get very precise doing estimations from their own previous experiences.
It is not clear when the humans started to use measurements, however we know that
ne of the first recorded measurement systems was in Egypt, around 5000 years ago.

The Egyptians used the cubit, coming from the Latin cubitum meaning “elbow”. Because each cubit was different from person to person, the Pharaoh came with a solution to use his cubit measure all over the territory. The administration created sticks which indicated the standard “cubit”. When the next pharaoh came he wanted a cubit measurement on his size so he ordered new sticks to be made. Soon the people wanted measure things smaller than a cubit so they came up with the palm measument (7 palms in a cubit) and the finger (4 fingers in a palm).
Other group of people, the Hebrews came up with their own system: span (the distance from the thumb to the little finger), the pace (2 royal cubits) and the royal foot.
The Greeks used the Egyptian measurements with their own adaptation.
The Romans used the uncial (today inch), the foot (12 uncia) and the yard (3 feet). The yard was also the distance from the nose to the tip of the middle finger of an out stretched arm.
In France alone there were more than 250 000 different measure units in use before of the introduction of the metric system.
The history of the metric system began in the Age of Enlightenment with simple notions
f length and weight taken from natural ones, and decimal multiples and fractions of
them. The system was so useful it became the standard of France and Europe in half a century. Other dimensions with unity ratios were added, and it went on to be adopted by the world.

The first practical realisation of the metric system came in 1799, during the French Revolution, when the existing system of measures, which had become impractical for trade, was replaced by a decimal system based on the kilogram and the metre. The basic units were taken from the natural world: the unit of length, the metre, was based
n the dimensions of the Earth, and the unit of mass, the kilogram, was based on the

mass of water having a volume of one litre or a cubic decimetre. Reference copies for both units were manufactured in platinum and remained the standards of measure for the next 90 years. After a period of reversion to the mesures usuelles due to unpopularity of the metric system, the metrication of France as well as much of Europe was complete by mid-century.

In the middle of the 19th century, James Clerk Maxwell put forward the concept of a coherent system where a small number of units of measure were defined as base units, and all other units of measure, called derived units, were defined in terms of the base units. Maxwell proposed three base units: length, mass and time. Advances in electromagnetism in the 19th century necessitated new units to be defined, and multiple incompatible systems of such units came into usage; none could be reconciled with the existing system of mechanical units. This impasse was resolved by Giovanni Giorgi, who in 1901 proved that a coherent system that incorporated electromagnetic units had to have an electromagnetic unit as a fourth base unit.

The seminal 1875 Treaty of the Metre resulted in the fashioning and distribution of metre and kilogram artefacts, the standards of the future coherent system that became the SI, and the creation of an international body Conférence générale des poids et mesures or CGPM to oversee systems of weights and measures based on them.

The Roman metric system was accepted through Europe and it is still in use today in the United States and UK, being called the Imperial metrical system. For reference of the units used, the table below can be observed.

Story of the metre

Though you've likely never given it much thought, a universally accepted unit of measurement like the humble meter is an amazing thing. It lets scientists separated by culture, language, race and even thousands of miles of geography work together on equations and problems like they were sitting next to each other. So how did this unit of measurement come to be? Well, before we discuss the meter, it's important to understand what came first. Prior to the meter, Europe's standard-ish unit of measurement was yards and inches. Though today there is an agreed exact length for an inch, go back a few hundred years and the definition was a little more lax. For example, for hundreds of years, the official definition of an inch was as follows. "three grains of barley, dry and round, placed end to end, lengthwise" For those of you who do not care for barley, in some places an inch was equal to the combined length of 12 poppy seeds instead. As discussed in the book, The Britannica Guide to Numbers and Measurement, the above definition was brought in during the rein of King Edward II in the 14th century. However, it is known that barleycorns were a standard unit of measurement for hundreds of years before this dating all the way back to the Anglo-Saxons. Also, earlier than this in 1150, King David of Scotland declared "the breadth of a man's thumb" as the standard unit of measurement, which like many of these other measurements, while practical in some respects, is massively stupid if you care for fine-point accuracy. However, throughout England, it was the barleycorn that reined supreme, virtually unchallenged for hundreds of years. Amazingly, a universally accepted value for the inch wasn't put into practise worldwide until July 1, 1959, after a number of countries collectively signed the International yard and pound agreement earlier that year in February. The countries, which included, the US, Canada, Britain, South Africa, New Zealand and Australia came to the
conclusion that an inch was to be officially and universally recognised as being 25.4 Millimeters.

So what made these fancy metric units so accurate that they were deemed better for measuring the length of an inch than barleycorns? Well it's because the meter was derived from something everyone on Earth could use for reference, the Earth itself.

The idea for the meter as a unit of measurement was first proposed during the French Revolution. As an example of just how necessary a universally accepted unit of measurement was needed, according to Ken Adler, author of, The Measure of All Things: The Seven-Year Odyssey that Transformed the World, there were around 250,000 different units of weights and measure in use in France during that time.

Now originally there were two proposed methods of discovering a standard unit of measurement; the first involved a pendulum with a half period of a single second. The alternate idea put forward was to find the length of one quadrant of the Earth's meridian and divide it by 10 million.

The French Academy Of Science opted for the latter due to the fact that gravity can vary ever so slightly depending on where you are on Earth, which would affect the swing of a pendulum and result in a standard, worldwide measurement being impossible to discern.

However, even though a method of deriving the unit was agreed upon in 1791, the exact distance of one quadrant of the Earth's meridian was not known at that time. To discover it, two notable French astronomers of the era, Pierre Méchain and Jean-Baptiste Delambre were sent in opposite directions from Paris to work out the length of the Earth's meridian between Dunkirk and Barcelona.

What should have taken the two men little more than a year, actually ended up taking 7 years, which is where the title of Ken Adler's book mentioned above came from. Why did it take so long? Loads of reasons not the least of which was that they were frequently arrested during their respective journeys- traipsing around surveying things presumably looked suspicious to authorities during the French Revolution.

They eventually got the needed measurements, but there was a problem- Méchain made a small, but nonetheless significant error very early on in the process of mapping the meridian, which wasn't discovered until later. He failed to take into account that the rotation
f the Earth made for a non-uniform shape. As a result, this
unintentionally threw off the entire result by a very small margin. This mistake proceed to haunt Méchain for the rest of his life, which wasn't
long. In the process of traveling and attempting to correct the error a few years later, he contracted yellow fever and died.
In the end, the mistake resulted in the first meter being off by approximately 1/5 of a millimeter from what the definition stated.

While the pair were off gallivanting around Europe though, the French still needed something to call a meter, so they had several platinum bars cast based on earlier, less exact calculations. When the pair returned and the exact-ish figure for a meter was calculated, the bar closest to this result was placed in a vault and it became the official standard of meter measurement in 1799. Later that year, the so dubbed, Metric System was implemented across France.

This platinum bar, known as the mètre des Archives was actually used as the literal measuring stick to which all other meters were measured for a few years. However, pressure quickly mounted on the scientific community to find a more effective, easily reproduced method of discerning the length of a meter as more and more countries began to implement the metric system.

After all, meter sticks being cast from the platinum original were prone to both damage and general wear and tear, resulting in no one being totally sure they were using the exact same definition as the other guy, which is kind of a bad thing when you're trying to do science that requires exacting measurements.

To combat this confusion and so that a universally agreed upon standard for the meter could be arranged, representatives from over two dozen countries were invited to attend The International Metre Commissionin Paris. These representative met several times from 1870- 1872 and decided on the casting of several new "metric prototypes" made of 90% platinum and 10% iridium, which would become the new standard everyone measured off of.
As time has progressed, we've gotten a bit more exacting about the process of measuring the meter. Starting in 1960, the official definition changed to:
…the length equal to 1,650,763.73 wavelengths in vacuum of the radiation corresponding to the transition between the levels 2p10 and
5d5 of the krypton 86 atom.
This lasted only until 1983 when the definition of a meter again changed as the technology to measure it continued to improve.
Today, the measuring of a meter has come full circle bringing us back to the original discarded suggestion of using time, though we have
gotten a bit more advanced than pendulums. Specifically, a meter is defined as being exactly:
The length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.
How does the modern version compare to the original measurements by Méchain and Delambre? It turns out their meter was only off from the modern definition by half a millimeter.

Algebra (from Arabic "al-jabr", literally meaning "reunion of broken parts") is one of the broad parts of mathematics, together with number theory, geometry and analysis. In its most general form, algebra is the study of mathematical symbols and the rules for manipulating these symbols; it is a unifying thread of almost all of mathematics. It includes everything from elementary equation solving to the study of abstractions such as groups, rings, and fields. The more basic parts of algebra are called elementary algebra; the more abstract parts are called abstract algebra or modern algebra. Elementary algebra is generally considered to be essential for any study of mathematics, science, or engineering, as well as such applications as medicine and economics. Abstract algebra is a major area in advanced mathematics, studied primarily by professional mathematicians.

The word algebra is also used in certain specialized ways. A special kind of mathematical object in abstract algebra is called an "algebra", and the word is used, for example, in the phrases linear algebra and algebraic topology.
A mathematician who does research in algebra is called an algebraist.

The word algebra comes from the Arabic ‫ الجبر‬(al-jabr lit. "the reunion of broken parts") from the title of the book Ilm al-jabr wa'l-muḳābala by the Persian mathematician and astronomer al-Khwarizmi. The word entered the English language during the fifteenth century, from either Spanish, Italian, or Medieval Latin. It originally referred to the surgical procedure of setting broken or dislocated bones. The mathematical meaning was first recorded in the sixteenth century.
